questions.q: Define microbodies and name the two main types found in plant cells, stating one key function of each.
questions.a: Microbodies are small, single-membrane-bound vesicles containing oxidative enzymes; the two main plant types are peroxisomes (contain catalase, glycolate oxidase – function in photorespiration/H₂O₂ detoxification) and glyoxysomes (contain isocitrate lyase, malate synthase – function in glyoxylate cycle converting fatty acids to carbohydrates during germination). A wrong answer (e.g., "microbodies are lysosomes" or "glyoxysomes do photosynthesis") reveals confusion between hydrolytic vs. oxidative organelles and ignorance of the glyoxylate cycle's role in gluconeogenesis.

questions.q: Why are peroxisomes considered essential for C3 plants during high light and temperature, even though they consume O₂ and release CO₂ without producing ATP?
questions.a: Peroxisomes recycle phosphoglycolate (a toxic byproduct of Rubisco oxygenase activity) back to 3-phosphoglycerate via the photorespiratory C₂ cycle, salvaging carbon and preventing inhibition of Calvin cycle; they also house catalase to detoxify H₂O₂ generated during this process. A wrong answer (e.g., "they produce ATP" or "they fix CO₂") shows fundamental misunderstanding of photorespiration as a salvage pathway, not an energy-yielding or carbon-fixing process.

questions.q: A student observes two types of granules in a plant cell under the microscope: one stains blue-black with iodine, the other dissolves in ethanol and stains red with Sudan III. Identify each inclusion, state its chemical nature, and explain why they are classified as cell inclusions rather than organelles.
questions.a: Blue-black iodine stain → starch grains (polysaccharide storage); red Sudan III stain → lipid droplets (triglyceride storage). Both are non-living, non-membranous, lack enzymes, and are not sites of metabolic reactions – they are ergastic substances. A wrong answer (e.g., "starch granules are plastids" or "lipid droplets are microbodies") reveals inability to distinguish membranous organelles from non-living inclusions based on structure and function.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the biogenesis and enzyme content of peroxisomes vs. lysosomes. Why can't peroxisomes be considered part of the endomembrane system?
questions.a: Peroxisomes: self-replicate by fission, import enzymes (catalase, oxidases) from cytosol via PTS1/PTS2 signals; lysosomes: formed from Golgi vesicles, contain acid hydrolases (proteases, lipases) synthesized on RER. Peroxisomes lack Golgi-derived membrane markers and do not receive vesicles from ER/Golgi, hence excluded from endomembrane system. A wrong answer (e.g., "both bud from Golgi" or "both have acid hydrolases") shows confusion between de novo organelle biogenesis and endomembrane trafficking.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Glyoxysomes are present only in germinating oil-rich seeds and disappear once the seedling becomes photosynthetic." Is it entirely correct? Justify with two specific biochemical reasons.
questions.a: Partially correct. Glyoxysomes are prominent in germinating oil seeds (castor, groundnut) where they run the glyoxylate cycle (isocitrate lyase + malate synthase) to convert acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation to succinate for gluconeogenesis. As photosynthesis establishes, glyoxysomes differentiate into peroxisomes (lose glyoxylate enzymes, gain photorespiratory enzymes). Two reasons: (1) Glyoxylate cycle enzymes are repressed by light/sugar signals; (2) Peroxisomal enzymes (glycolate oxidase) are induced for photorespiration. A wrong answer (e.g., "they stay forever" or "they become mitochondria") reveals ignorance of organelle interconversion and metabolic switching during seedling development.

questions.q: Design a simple histochemical experiment using a germinating groundnut seed to demonstrate the transition from glyoxysomes to peroxisomes over a 7-day period. Specify the stains/assays, time points, and expected observations.
questions.a: Day 0 (dry seed), Day 2, Day 4, Day 7. Assays: (1) Catalase activity (H₂O₂ decomposition → O₂ bubbles) – increases steadily. (2) Isocitrate lyase activity (spectrophotometric NADH consumption) – peaks Day 2-3, absent by Day 7. (3) Glycolate oxidase activity (O₂ consumption with glycolate) – low early, high Day 7. (4) Electron microscopy for crystalloid core (glyoxysome marker) – present early, absent late. Expected: Early high glyoxylate enzymes + crystalloids; late high photorespiratory enzymes + no crystalloids. A poor answer (only one assay, no time course, or confusing stains) shows inability to design multi-parameter temporal experiments for organelle differentiation.
